content: Thiram, also known as tetramethylthiuram disulfide, is an ectoparasiticide primarily used to prevent fungal diseases in seeds and crops. It is also employed as an animal repellent to protect fruit trees and ornamental plants from damage caused by rabbits, rodents, and deer. Thiram is effective against various plant diseases, including stem gall of coriander, damping-off, smut of millet, and neck rot of onion. Historically, it has been used in humans for the treatment of scabies, as a sunscreen, and as a bactericide, either applied directly to the skin or incorporated into soap formulations. Chemically, thiram is classified as a sulfur-based fungicide. It is highly soluble in organic solvents such as chloroform, acetone, and ether. Thiram is available in various formulations, including dust, flowable liquids, wettable powders, water-dispersible granules, and water suspension mixtures, often combined with other fungicides. In soil, thiram exhibits low mobility, particularly in clay-rich or high-organic-matter soils. It has a short in-soil half-life of approximately 15 days and a strong tendency to adhere to soil particles, making it unlikely to contaminate groundwater. Thiram is moderately toxic when ingested but poses a higher toxicity risk when inhaled. It is an irritant to the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract and is known to act as a skin sensitizer. Inhalation of thiram can lead to symptoms such as itching, a scratchy throat, hoarseness, sneezing, coughing, nasal or throat inflammation, bronchitis, dizziness, headaches, fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, and other gastrointestinal complaints. These include drowsiness, confusion, reduced libido, incoordination, slurred speech, and generalized weakness.
